You are the EVALUATOR hardener (red team) for repo /Users/skodi/Desktop/take-home-assessment. WRITE CODE. Python 3 stdlib only, must run on Python 3.8+. Work autonomously, then return a short report.

## Context
Assignment: `./evaluate OPTIMIZER` tests any optimizer with the CLI `OPTIMIZER program.mini schema.json` (prints an optimized MiniVM program). Exit 0 if no defects, non-zero if any. A defect = an optimized program whose results differ from the original's: same results required on any data satisfying the schema's constraints; order doesn't matter unless the input program specifies it; numbers within 1e-6 relative; if the original errors, anything goes; optimizer must take ≤ 1 s per program. Evaluator must finish in ≤ 2 minutes and may use bin/minivm. Read: `BUILD_PLAN.md` §4 (evaluator design), §6 (rubric), §7 (unclear rules Q1–Q10 and chosen defaults), §10; `notes/tricky_rules.md`; `minivm-takehome/docs/**`; the prototype `prototype_code/evaluator_agent/{eval-proto.py,fake_opt.py,meta_eval.py,tricky_checks.py}`.
A production evaluator already exists (orchestrator wrote it, committed d7c30ff): `./evaluate` -> `evaluator/main.py`, with `evaluator/vm.py` (platform binary runner), `evaluator/datagen.py` (constraint-respecting tricky data, any schema), `evaluator/progen.py` (random legacy-style program generator + random schemas), `evaluator/compare.py` (parser, output_ordered, static output types, tie-aware comparison by instrumenting the original to also output sort keys, TOPK/SLICE cut-off ties => WARN). Current results: identity optimizer 0 defects (quick 777 checks 5 s; full ~3800 checks 23 s); naive_opt.sh caught.

## Your job (iterate with scripts)
1. Port the meta-eval: `tools/fakes.py` (fake optimizers MODE prog schema: at least the prototype's 8 honest + 11 buggy, plus NEW ones you design from the spec only, e.g. honest: tie-reordering after stable sort with ties where the original's tie order is not "specified" — decide carefully, HJOIN<->NLJOIN, DCE, register rename, reformat/case; buggy: drop NVL, GE->GT, drop NOT ISNULL filter, swap join sides, TOPK n-1, remove a DIV-guarding filter (adds an error), dedup a no-key table, filter pushed above a SLICE, wrong GSUM->GCOUNT, change string literal case, 1e-5 drift, emit invalid program, sleep 1.5 s) and `tools/meta_eval.py` that runs ./evaluate --quick against each fake and reports CAUGHT/MISSED/OK/FALSE-ALARM to `runs/meta_report.md`. Targets: 100% buggy caught, 0 false alarms.
2. Fix evaluator weaknesses you find (misses or false alarms): data generator coverage (plant literals, ties, NULL/'' keys, empty tables, rows > TOPK limits, data that makes originals error), comparator rules, order/tie detection, instrumentation robustness, random schema/program generator validity (count how many generated programs are skipped on every dataset / always empty output — keep only useful ones, or improve generation), determinism (same seed -> identical report), and timing (full run < 60 s target, hard < 120 s with watchdog). Verify `./evaluate` works when invoked from another cwd and with a relative optimizer path, and that it never writes files outside a temp dir except ./eval_out repros.
3. Port `prototype_code/evaluator_agent/tricky_checks.py` ideas into `tools/eval_selftest.py` covering compare.py rules (BOOL vs INT, STR '1.0' vs '1.00' typed, numeric tolerance, tie blocks, ordered detection), runnable in < 10 s.
Run `./evaluate minivm-takehome/optimize`, `./evaluate prototype_code/optimizer_agent/hand_opt.sh` (must be 0 defects) and `./evaluate prototype_code/optimizer_agent/naive_opt.sh` (must catch) after each change.

## Logging (required)
Append one row per iteration to `runs/evaluator_iterations.md` (create with header):
`| # | Time (UTC, date -u +%H:%M) | Approach (ELI5, 1-2 sentences) | Buggy caught | False alarms | Checks / wall s (quick, full) | Takeaway (< 5 sentences) |`

## Boundaries
You own ONLY: `evaluator/**`, `./evaluate`, `tools/fakes.py`, `tools/meta_eval.py`, `tools/eval_selftest.py`, `runs/meta_report.md`, `runs/evaluator_iterations.md`. You must NOT read or import anything under `optimizer/` or `./optimize` (independence: evaluator must be black-box). Another agent is concurrently building the optimizer and running `./evaluate` constantly: keep `./evaluate`'s CLI (`OPTIMIZER [--seed S] [--quick] [--json OUT] [--keep DIR] [-v]`) stable, and make each edit leave it working (run `./evaluate minivm-takehome/optimize --quick` right after edits). Another agent owns `tests/` (it may add test programs under tests/cases which ./evaluate picks up).
Git: commit as you go, ONLY your paths: `git add evaluator evaluate tools/fakes.py tools/meta_eval.py tools/eval_selftest.py runs/meta_report.md runs/evaluator_iterations.md && git commit -m "..."` (retry if .git/index.lock exists). Never reset/amend/force. End messages with:

Generated with [Snowflake CoCo](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/cortex-code/cortex-code)

Co-authored-by: Snowflake CoCo <noreply@snowflake.com>

## Final report (your only message back)
Iteration table rows, final meta-eval verdict table (each fake: expected, result, defect count), quick/full wall times, any rule decisions you made (and why), remaining known gaps, commit hashes.

[MiniVM docs](README.md) › Language

# Language

This page gives the syntax of MiniVM programs: lines, comments, opcodes,
registers, operands and literals.

## Programs

A program is straight-line: its instructions run once each, in order. Each
line holds one instruction. A `;` starts a comment, which runs to the end of
the line; a line may hold only a comment, or be blank. Spaces and tabs are
interchangeable: they separate the opcode from its operands, and may indent a
line or surround an operand.

```text
; Ids and amounts of orders over 100.
load   id, orders.o_id
load   amt, orders.o_amt
gt     m, amt, 100      ; NULL where o_amt is NULL
idx    i, m
gather a, id, i
gather b, amt, i
out    a, b
```

The program must end with its only `OUT`; see [Program rules](running.md#program
-rules).                                                                        
## Instructions

An instruction is an opcode followed by comma-separated operands:

```text
OP dest, operand, ...
```

Opcodes are case-insensitive: `gt`, `Gt` and `GT` are the same instruction.
So are the keywords `NULL`, `TRUE`, `FALSE`, `ASC`, `DESC`, `NF`, `NL` and
`NULLEQ`.
Each opcode's operands are given on its page in the
[instruction reference](instructions/README.md).

## Registers

Register names are identifiers, such as `r1`, `amt` or `_t0`: a letter or `_`,
followed by letters, digits and `_`. Register names are case-sensitive, and a
keyword can't be a register name. A register holds a column or a group set
([Values](values.md#columns-and-group-sets)) and can be overwritten.

## Operands

An operand is one of:

| Operand | Example | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| register | `amt` | every instruction |
| literal | `100.00` | element-wise instructions, `FILL`, integer operands such 
as `LEFT`'s `n` |                                                               | `table.column` | `orders.o_amt` | [`LOAD`](instructions/columns.md#load) |
| sort key | `amt DESC NL` | [`SORT`, `TOPK`](instructions/sorting.md#sort-keys)
 |                                                                              | `NULLEQ` | `NULLEQ` | [`NLJOIN`, `HJOIN`](instructions/joins.md#nljoin-hjoin) 
|                                                                               
## Literals

| Literal | Type | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `42`, `-7` | INT | must fit in 128 bits |
| `12.50` | NUM | must be exact, in the [NUM range](values.md#num-range) |
| `'it''s'` | STR | a quote inside the string is written twice |
| `#2024-01-31#` | DATE | years 0001 to 9999 |
| `NULL` | NULL | |
| `TRUE`, `FALSE` | BOOL | |

A literal stands for that value at every row.

## Integer operands

Some operands must be integer literals rather than registers: `n` and `len`
(`LEFT`, `SUBSTR`, `SLICE`, `TOPK`) are non-negative, and `SUBSTR`'s `start` is
at least 1. They may be arbitrarily large; a count larger than the input means
all of it.
[MiniVM docs](README.md) › Values

# Values

This page describes MiniVM's values and types, what a register holds, and how
values are ordered and compared.

## Types

| Type | Values | Literal |
|---|---|---|
| INT | exact 128-bit integer; a result outside -2^127 .. 2^127-1 is an error | 
`42` |                                                                          | NUM | decimal: see [NUM range](#num-range) | `12.50` |
| STR | string | `'it''s'` |
| DATE | calendar date | `#2024-01-31#` |
| BOOL | `FALSE` or `TRUE` | `TRUE` |

`NULL` is a value of its own, written `NULL`. Unless an instruction says
otherwise, an element-wise result is `NULL` when any operand is `NULL`
([element-wise instructions](instructions/README.md#element-wise-instructions)).

Literal syntax is in [Literals](language.md#literals). Stored columns have
type INT, NUM, STR or DATE ([table sets](running.md#table-sets)).

## NUM range

A NUM is below 1e28 in magnitude and has at most 28 digits after the point,
and its digits without the point, read as an integer, are at most
2^96 - 1 = 79228162514264337593543950335: 28 or 29 significant digits.
A NUM keeps its digits after the point, so `1.0` and `1.00` are equal but
print differently.

A NUM literal or stored value must be such a number exactly; trailing zeros
after the point are dropped as far as needed. A NUM result is rounded half to
even to the most digits after the point that fit, and a result of magnitude
1e28 or more is the error `numeric overflow`. Where an INT meets a NUM in
arithmetic, and in `DIV`, an INT operand above 2^96 - 1 in magnitude is that
error too, even if the result would fit.

## Columns and group sets

A register holds either:

- a **column**: a vector of values; or
- a **group set**: a grouping of rows, made by
  [`GROUP`](instructions/grouping.md#group) or [`GALL`](instructions/grouping.md
#gall)                                                                            and read by the other [grouping instructions](instructions/grouping.md).

Registers can be overwritten.

## Ordering

These instructions compare values:

- [`EQ`, `NE`, `LT`, `LE`, `GT`, `GE`](instructions/logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) 
and [`IS`](instructions/logic.md#is)                                            - [`SORT`](instructions/sorting.md#sort) and [`TOPK`](instructions/sorting.md#to
pk)                                                                             - the joins [`NLJOIN`, `HJOIN`](instructions/joins.md#nljoin-hjoin)
- [`GMIN`, `GMAX`](instructions/grouping.md#gmin-gmax)

They order values as follows:

| Values | Order |
|---|---|
| INT and NUM | by numeric value, exactly at any magnitude; INT and NUM mix |
| STR | by bytes |
| DATE | by date |
| BOOL | `FALSE < TRUE` |

Comparing any other mix of types, such as STR with INT or DATE with NUM, is an
error.

String comparison is exact: there is no case folding, and trailing spaces
count, so `'ab'` and `'ab '` differ, as do `'ab'` and `'AB'`.

How each instruction treats `NULL` is given on its page; for sorts, see
[sort keys](instructions/sorting.md#sort-keys).
[MiniVM docs](README.md) › Running

# Running

This page gives the rules every program must follow, what happens on an error,
how to run a program with `bin/minivm`, and the JSON format of the tables it
reads.

## Program rules

The last instruction must be the program's only [`OUT`](instructions/columns.md#
out).                                                                           
| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| instructions per program | at most 20,000 |
| values held by one register | at most 4,000,000 (a join's output counts) |
| values held by all registers together | at most 64,000,000; a long string coun
ts as several values (about 1 per 32 bytes) |                                   | work per run | roughly 300,000,000 [cycles](cycles.md); see below |
| rows per table | at most 10,000 |
| program file | at most 4 MiB |
| table-set file | at most 32 MiB and 2,000,000 JSON values |

The work limit stops runaway programs. It counts a run's cycles, but `HJOIN`
and `GROUP` and copying long strings use it up faster than their cycles
suggest, so such programs stop somewhat sooner. Exceeding it, like any other
limit, is an error. It has no effect on the cycles reported for a run that
finishes.

## Errors

Any error stops the program. No result is printed; the error goes to stderr
and `bin/minivm` exits with status 1.

## Command line

```sh
bin/minivm PROGRAM.mini TABLES.json
bin/minivm --schema TABLES.json
```

runs the program in `PROGRAM.mini` on the [table set](#table-sets) in
`TABLES.json`. On success it prints one line of JSON to stdout and exits 0:

```json
{"ncols": N, "rows": [...], "cycles": C}
```

- `ncols` is the number of `OUT` operands.
- `rows` is the result, one array of `ncols` values per row.
  `NULL` is `null` and a BOOL is `true` or `false`. An INT is a JSON integer,
  or a string of its digits outside -2^63 .. 2^63-1. A NUM is a string that keep
s                                                                                 its digits after the point (`"250.00"`), a STR a string, and a DATE a string
  `"YYYY-MM-DD"`.
- `cycles` is the program's cost ([Cycles](cycles.md)).

| Exit status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | success; the result is on stdout |
| 1 | error; the message is on stderr |
| 2 | wrong number of arguments; a usage line is on stderr |

With the program from [Language](language.md#programs) saved as
`over100.mini` and the [example table set](#example) as `orders.json`:

```sh
$ bin/minivm over100.mini orders.json
{"ncols":2,"rows":[[1,"250.00"]],"cycles":42}
```

`bin/minivm --schema TABLES.json` prints the table set's [schema file](#schema-f
iles)                                                                           as one line of JSON instead of running a program.

A program that compares a DATE with an INT stops with an error:

```text
LOAD d, orders.o_date
GT   m, d, 5
OUT  m
```

```sh
$ bin/minivm bad.mini orders.json
error: line 2: GT: expected a number, got DATE
```

## Table sets

A table set is a JSON object mapping each table name to its columns and rows:

```json
{"<table>": {"columns": [{"name": "c", "type": "INT|NUM|STR|DATE"}], "rows": [[.
..], ...]}}                                                                     ```

- Table and column names are identifiers (letters, digits and `_`, not starting
  with a digit), compared without regard to case. Duplicate names are an error.
- `columns` lists each column's `name` and `type`, one of `INT`, `NUM`, `STR`, `
DATE`.                                                                          - `rows` lists each row as an array of values, one per column, in column order.
  A table without `rows` is empty.
- A table may also declare [constraints](#constraints).
- Any key other than those shown or listed there is an error, as is a repeated k
ey.                                                                             - A table holds at most 10,000 rows.
- INT values are JSON integers that fit in 32 bits.
- NUM values may be JSON numbers or strings. They must be exact, in the
  [NUM range](values.md#num-range).
- Dates are strings `"YYYY-MM-DD"`, years 0001 to 9999.
- JSON `null` is `NULL`.

A program reads a stored column with `LOAD d, table.column` ([`LOAD`](instructio
ns/columns.md#load)).                                                           
### Constraints

A table may declare what its rows guarantee. `bin/minivm` checks every declared
constraint when it reads the table set, and a table set that breaks one is an er
ror.                                                                            
| Key | Example | Guarantee |
|---|---|---|
| `key` | `["l_order", "l_no"]` | the columns are never `NULL`, and no two rows 
agree on all of them |                                                          | `not_null` | `["p_price"]` | the columns are never `NULL` |
| `refs` | `{"l_prod": "products.p_id"}` | every non-NULL value of the column is
 a value of the other column, which must be its table's whole `key` and have the same type (INT and NUM may refer to each other) |                              | `check` | `{"l_qty": [1, 500]}` | every non-NULL value lies between the bounds
, inclusive; `null` leaves a side open; INT, NUM and DATE columns only |        | `sorted` | `["l_order", "l_no"]` | the rows are stored in ascending order of t
he columns, as `ASC NF` sorts them |                                            
Values are compared as in [Ordering](values.md#ordering), so NUM keys `1.0` and
`1.00` are the same key. Column names in constraints are compared without regard
to case, and naming a column twice in one constraint is an error. A table may re
fer to itself.                                                                  
```json
{
  "orders": {"columns": [{"name": "o_id", "type": "INT"}], "key": ["o_id"], "row
s": [[1], [2]]},                                                                  "lines": {
    "columns": [{"name": "l_order", "type": "INT"}, {"name": "l_qty", "type": "I
NT"}],                                                                              "refs": {"l_order": "orders.o_id"}, "check": {"l_qty": [1, null]}, "sorted":
 ["l_order"],                                                                       "rows": [[1, 3], [1, 1], [2, 5]]
  }
}
```

```json

    "columns": [
      {"name": "o_id",     "type": "INT"},
      {"name": "o_amt",    "type": "NUM"},
      {"name": "o_date",   "type": "DATE"},
      {"name": "o_status", "type": "STR"}

      [2, "99.5",   "2024-02-01", ""],
      [3, null,     "2024-02-03", null]

}
```

`bin/minivm --schema TABLES.json` describes a table set without its rows: each t
able's                                                                          columns and [constraints](#constraints), as in the table set, plus a `stats` obj

```json
{"<table>": {"columns": [...], "key": [...], ..., "stats": {"rows": N, "columns"
: {"<column>": {"nulls": N, "distinct": N, "min": v, "max": v, "common": [[v, N], ...], ...}}}}}                                                                ```

# Tricky rules: what bin/minivm does and how the evaluator handles it

Every item was checked with `bin/minivm`. They are encoded as 56 repeatable chec
ks in                                                                           `prototype_code/evaluator_agent/tricky_checks.py` (56/56 pass).

## Parsing
- **Case:** opcodes and keywords ignore case (`sort` = `SORT` = `SoRt`, `asc nf`
 = `ASC NF`). Register names are case-sensitive (`a` ≠ `A`, `s` ≠ `S`). The order detector upper-cases opcodes only.                                            - **Literals:** `;` and `,` inside a string literal are data, not a comment or a
 separator. `''` is an escaped quote.                                           - **Layout:** CRLF line endings, blank lines and comments after `OUT` are all fi
ne. `OUT` with no operands is an error.                                         
## Output JSON has no types
- **Text looks alike:** STR `"2.00"`, `"2024-01-31"` and `"1e5"` print exactly l
ike NUM, DATE and plain text. Only BOOL is distinct, because it prints unquoted `true`/`false`.                                                                 - **Number formats:** minivm prints numbers only as `-?\d+(\.\d+)?` (JSON intege
rs, or strings beyond ±2^63). The comparator therefore treats only that exact text as a number. **Bug fixed:** it used to parse `'1.0 '` and `'1e5'` as numbers, which hid TRIM-style bugs.                                                     - **BOOL vs INT:** Python has `True == 1`. **Bug fixed:** `true` vs `1` and `fal
se` vs `0` used to compare as equal.                                            - **Negative zero:** `NEG 0.0` prints `"-0.0"` but `MUL 0.0, -1` prints `"0"`. T
he two are equal by value, so this is not a defect.                             - **Remaining ambiguity:** STR `'1.0'` vs STR `'1.00'` compares as equal numbers
. This can't be fixed without column types (documented).                        
## Tolerance (one-pager: numbers within 1e-6 relative)
- **Large INTs:** this tolerance applies to INTs too. `10000000` vs `10000001` p
asses. That follows the spec, but it means off-by-one errors on very large counts go undetected.                                                                - **Zero:** the tolerance is purely relative, so `0` vs `0.0000001` is a defect.
 A correct optimizer doesn't change arithmetic, so this is fine.                
## Row order
- **When order counts:** rows are compared **in order** whenever the original's 
output order comes from a SORT or TOPK, and as a multiset otherwise.            - **Order detector:** decided by a data-flow pass over the original program. It 
covers filters, the right side of a join, GROUP numbering after a sort, register overwrites, sorts whose result is never output, and comments.                  - **Effect:** before this rule, the reversed-rows bug was missed and the sort-fl
ip and dropped-tie-break bugs were barely caught (4 and 2 defects). Now all three are caught (172, 134 and 19 defects), with 0 false alarms on the 8 honest fakes.                                                                              - **Known limit:** rows that tie on the sort keys are also compared in order. SO
RT is stable, so ties keep their input order. An optimizer that legally reorders ties would be flagged. None of the honest fakes do this. It's open question Q1 in the plan.                                                                    
## Empty and degenerate data
- **Empty tables:** GROUP gives **0 rows**, but GALL gives **1 row `[0, NULL]`**
. An optimizer that swaps them is wrong on empty data only.                     - **Errors on empty columns:** `DIV` by 0 and type errors never fire on empty or
 all-NULL columns, so whether a program errors depends on its data.             - **Empty GALL:** GFIRST gives NULL, and GATHER with a NULL index is an error.

## Speed
- **Platform binary:** calling `bin/minivm-macos-aarch64` directly takes 8.3 ms 
per run, against 38.6 ms through the `bin/minivm` wrapper. The wrapper spawns a shell and runs `xattr` every time. Output is identical on all examples.         - **Evaluator:** it now resolves the platform binary itself, the same way the wr
apper does, and clears the quarantine flag once. A full evaluation dropped from 8.4 s to **1.7 s**. `MINIVM=...` overrides the choice.                          - **Determinism:** the same program and data give byte-identical output across r
uns.

m() < 0.5 else "")

            self.emit("LEFT", w, z, rng.choice([8, 12, 20, 40]), comment="sheet 
column width")                                                                              out.append(Col(w, "STR"))
        if len(nums) >= 2 and rng.random() < 0.5:
            a, b = rng.sample(nums, 2)
            x = self.fresh("v")
            self.emit("MUL", x, a.reg, b.reg)
            out.append(Col(x, "NUM" if "NUM" in (a.type, b.type) else "INT"))
        if nums and rng.random() < 0.15:
            a, b = rng.choice(nums), rng.choice(nums)
            x = self.fresh("q")
            self.emit("DIV", x, a.reg, b.reg, comment="ratio")
            out.append(Col(x, "NUM"))
        if rng.random() < 0.3 and cols:   # dead "display copy"
            c = rng.choice(cols)
            if c.type == "STR":
                self.emit("UPPER", self.fresh("d"), c.reg, comment="display copy
")                                                                                          elif c.type == "DATE":
                self.emit("DOW", self.fresh("d"), c.reg, comment="weekday split 
(removed)")                                                                             return out

    # ---- joins
    def join_options(self, cols):
        opts = []
        for c in cols:
            if not c.table:
                continue
            for k, v in self.s[c.table].get("refs", {}).items():
                if k.lower() == c.name.lower():
                    pt, pc = v.split(".")
                    pt = next(t for t in self.s if t.lower() == pt.lower())
                    opts.append(("fk", c, pt, pc))
        tabs = {c.table for c in cols if c.table}
        for t in self.s:
            for k, v in self.s[t].get("refs", {}).items():
                pt, pc = v.split(".")
                for c in cols:
                    if c.table and c.table.lower() == pt.lower() and c.name.lowe
r() == pc.lower() and t not in tabs:                                                                    opts.append(("rev", c, t, k))
        for c in cols:                    # same-type columns without refs (e.g.
 no-key tables)                                                                             for t in self.s:
                if t in tabs:
                    continue
                for tc in self.tcols(t):
                    if tc["type"] == c.type and c.type == "INT" and tc["name"].l
ower().endswith(c.name.lower()[-2:]) \                                                                      and self.rng.random() < 0.05:
                        opts.append(("loose", c, t, tc["name"]))
        return opts

    def join(self, cols):
        opts = self.join_options(cols)
        if not opts:
            return cols, False
        kind, c, t, tc = self.rng.choice(opts)
        other = self.load_table(t)
        oc = next(o for o in other if o.name.lower() == tc.lower())
        li, ri = self.fresh("j"), self.fresh("j")
        op = "NLJOIN" if self.rng.random() < 0.15 else "HJOIN"
        self.emit(op, li, ri, c.reg, oc.reg)
        return self.gather_all(cols, li) + self.gather_all(other, ri), True

    # ---- idioms
    def self_join_agg(self, cols):
        """per row: aggregate over the rows sharing a key (correlated subquery s
tyle)."""                                                                               rng = self.rng
        keys = [c for c in cols if c.type in ("STR", "INT") and c.table]
        vals = [c for c in cols if c.type in NUMT]
        if not keys or not vals:
            return cols, None
        k, v = rng.choice(keys), rng.choice(vals)
        kr = k.reg
        if k.type == "STR" and rng.random() < 0.6:
            a = self.fresh("n")
            self.emit("NULLIFE", a, k.reg)
            b = self.fresh("t")
            self.emit("RTRIM", b, a)
            kr = self.fresh("u")
            self.emit("UPPER", kr, b)
        a, b = self.fresh("a"), self.fresh("b")
        self.emit("HJOIN", a, b, kr, kr, comment="every pair with the same key")
        vb = self.fresh()
        self.emit("GATHER", vb, v.reg, b)
        g = self.fresh("g")
        mode = rng.choice(["max", "min", "cnt_less"])
        if mode == "cnt_less":
            va = self.fresh()
            self.emit("GATHER", va, v.reg, a)
            h = self.fresh("hit")
            self.emit("LT", h, vb, va)
            one = self.fresh("one")
            self.emit("IF", one, h, 1, 0)
            self.emit("GROUP", g, a)
            agg = self.fresh("cnt")
            self.emit("GSUM", agg, g, one)
            t = "INT"
        else:
            self.emit("GROUP", g, a)
            agg = self.fresh(mode)
            self.emit("GMAX" if mode == "max" else "GMIN", agg, g, vb)
            t = v.type
        f = self.fresh("f")
        self.emit("GFIRST", f, g)
        row = self.fresh("row")
        self.emit("GATHER", row, a, f)
        out = self.gather_all(cols, row)
        return out + [Col(agg, t)], agg

    # ---- endings
    def sort_keys(self, cols, n):
        ks = self.rng.sample(cols, min(n, len(cols)))
        return [f"{c.reg} {self.rng.choice(['ASC', 'DESC'])} {self.rng.choice(['
NF', 'NL'])}" for c in ks]                                                      
    def finish(self, cols):
        rng = self.rng
        kind = rng.choice(["proj", "sort", "sort", "topn", "group", "gall"])
        out = rng.sample(cols, min(len(cols), rng.randint(1, 4)))
        if kind == "proj":
            self.emit("OUT", *[c.reg for c in out])
        elif kind in ("sort", "topn"):
            keys = self.sort_keys(cols, rng.choice([1, 2, 2]))
            p = self.fresh("s")
            self.emit("SORT", p, *keys)
            outs = self.gather_all(out, p)
            if kind == "topn":
                i = self.fresh("k")
                self.emit("IOTA", i, outs[0].reg)
                self.emit("SLICE", i, i, rng.choice([1, 3, 5, 10]))
                outs = self.gather_all(outs, i)
            self.emit("OUT", *[c.reg for c in outs])
        elif kind == "group":
            gk = rng.choice([c for c in cols if c.type != "BOOL"])
            g = self.fresh("g")
            self.emit("GROUP", g, gk.reg)
            f = self.fresh("f")
            self.emit("GFIRST", f, g)
            key = self.fresh("key")
            self.emit("GATHER", key, gk.reg, f)
            aggs = [key]
            nums = [c for c in cols if c.type in NUMT]
            for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 3)):
                a = self.fresh("agg")
                choice = rng.choice(["GCOUNT", "GSUM", "GMIN", "GMAX", "GCOUNTV"
])                                                                                              if choice == "GCOUNT":
                    self.emit("GCOUNT", a, g)
                elif choice == "GCOUNTV":
                    self.emit("GCOUNTV", a, g, rng.choice(cols).reg)
                elif nums:
                    self.emit(choice, a, g, rng.choice(nums).reg)
                else:
                    self.emit("GCOUNT", a, g)
                aggs.append(a)
            if rng.random() < 0.7:
                s = self.fresh("s")
                self.emit("SORT", s, f"{key} ASC NF")
                outs = []
                for a in aggs:
                    r = self.fresh()
                    self.emit("GATHER", r, a, s)
                    outs.append(r)
                aggs = outs
            self.emit("OUT", *aggs)
        else:
            nums = [c for c in cols if c.type in NUMT] or cols
            g = self.fresh("g")
            self.emit("GALL", g, nums[0].reg)
            a, b = self.fresh("tot"), self.fresh("n")
            if nums[0].type in NUMT:
                self.emit("GSUM", a, g, nums[0].reg)
            else:
                self.emit("GCOUNTV", a, g, nums[0].reg)
            self.emit("GCOUNT", b, g)
            self.emit("OUT", a, b)

    def build(self):
        rng = self.rng
        tabs = [t for t in self.s if self.s[t].get("stats", {}).get("rows", 1) >
 0] or list(self.s)                                                                     t0 = rng.choice(tabs)
        self.lines.append(f"; generated legacy-style program over {t0}")
        cols = self.load_table(t0)
        sp = self.s[t0]
        if sp.get("sorted") and rng.random() < 0.3:   # sort on a sorted table: 
identity                                                                                    sk = [next(c for c in cols if c.name.lower() == k.lower()) for k in 
sp["sorted"]]                                                                               p = self.fresh("s")
            self.emit("SORT", p, *[f"{c.reg} ASC NF" for c in sk], comment="keep
 the stored order stable")                                                                  cols = self.gather_all(cols, p)
        if rng.random() < 0.3:
            cols = self.filt(cols)
        late_filter = rng.random() < 0.7
        for _ in range(rng.choice([0, 1, 1, 2, 3])):
            cols, _ = self.join(cols)
            if len(cols) > 40:
                break
        extra = self.computed(cols)
        cols = cols + extra
        if rng.random() < 0.25:
            cols, _ = self.self_join_agg(cols)
        if rng.random() < 0.3:      # sort, then filter (filter-before-sort is e
quivalent)                                                                                  keys = self.sort_keys(cols, 2)
            p = self.fresh("s")
            self.emit("SORT", p, *keys, comment="audit trail order")
            cols = self.gather_all(cols, p)
        if late_filter:
            cols = self.filt(cols)
        self.finish(cols)
        return "\n".join(self.lines) + "\n"


def gen_program(schema, rng):
    return P(schema, rng).build()


def random_schema(rng, name="gen"):
    """A random schema (columns + constraints) for generalization tests; stats c
ome from bin/minivm later."""                                                       ntab = rng.randint(2, 4)
    tables = {}
    for ti in range(ntab):
        t = f"{name}_t{ti}"
        cols = [{"name": f"c{ti}_id", "type": "INT"}]
        for ci in range(rng.randint(2, 5)):
            cols.append({"name": f"c{ti}_{ci}", "type": rng.choice(["INT", "NUM"
, "STR", "STR", "DATE"])})                                                              spec = {"columns": cols}
        if rng.random() < 0.8:
            spec["key"] = [cols[0]["name"]]
        nn = [c["name"] for c in cols[1:] if rng.random() < 0.3]
        if nn:
            spec["not_null"] = nn
        chk = {}
        for c in cols[1:]:
            if c["type"] == "INT" and rng.random() < 0.3:
                chk[c["name"]] = [rng.randint(-5, 1), rng.choice([None, 100])]
        if chk:
            spec["check"] = chk
        if ti > 0:
            parents = [p for p in tables if "key" in tables[p]]
            if parents and rng.random() < 0.8:
                p = rng.choice(parents)
                fk = {"name": f"c{ti}_fk", "type": "INT"}
                cols.append(fk)
                spec["refs"] = {fk["name"]: f"{p}.{tables[p]['key'][0]}"}
                if rng.random() < 0.5:
                    spec.setdefault("not_null", []).append(fk["name"])
                if rng.random() < 0.3:
                    spec["sorted"] = [fk["name"]]
        tables[t] = spec
    return tables

def run_optimizer(optimizer, prog, schema, outdir):
    t = time.monotonic()
    try:
        r = __import__("subprocess").run([optimizer, prog, schema], capture_outp
ut=True, text=True,                                                                                                      timeout=10 * OPT_LIMIT_S)
    except Exception as e:  # timeout or not executable
        return None, f"optimizer failed: {e}", time.monotonic() - t
    dt = time.monotonic() - t
    if r.returncode != 0 or not r.stdout.strip():
        return None, f"optimizer failed (exit {r.returncode}): {r.stderr.strip()
[:200]}", dt                                                                        out = os.path.join(outdir, os.path.basename(prog))
    open(out, "w").write(r.stdout)
    if dt > OPT_LIMIT_S:
        return out, f"optimizer took {dt:.2f} s (> {OPT_LIMIT_S} s)", dt
    return out, None, dt


class Program:
    def __init__(self, path, schema_path, schema, work):
        self.path, self.schema_path = path, schema_path
        self.name = os.path.relpath(path, REPO) if path.startswith(REPO) else os
.path.basename(path)                                                                    self.prog = C.parse(open(path).read())
        self.ordered = C.output_ordered(self.prog)
        self.types = C.out_types(self.prog, schema)
        self.cutoff = any(op in ("TOPK", "SLICE") for op, _ in self.prog)
        self.inst = None
        if self.ordered:
            text = C.instrument(self.prog)
            if text:
                self.inst = os.path.join(work, f"keys_{len(os.listdir(work))}_{o
s.path.basename(path)}")                                                                        open(self.inst, "w").write(text)


def check(p, opt, data):
    a, ea = vm.run(p.path, data)
    if a is None:
        return "SKIP", ea, None
    b, eb = vm.run(opt, data)
    if b is None:
        return "DEFECT", "optimized program errors: " + eb, (a["cycles"], None)
    keyed = None
    st, detail = C.compare(a, b, p.ordered, p.types, None, p.cutoff)
    if st == "DEFECT" and p.ordered and p.inst:
        k, _ = vm.run(p.inst, data)
        if k is not None:
            keyed = k["rows"]
            st, detail = C.compare(a, b, p.ordered, p.types, keyed, p.cutoff)
    return st, detail, (a["cycles"], b["cycles"])

}".replace(".", "_"))                                                               os.makedirs(d, exist_ok=True)

[MiniVM docs](../README.md) › Instructions

# Instructions

This page states the conventions shared by all instructions and indexes every op
code. Cycle costs are summarized in [Cycles](../cycles.md).                     
## Notation

Each instruction is shown as `OP` followed by its operands:

- `d` is the destination register (`li`, `ri` for joins, `g` for group sets).
- `a`, `b`, `c`, `s`, `x`, `y` are source operands: `c` is a condition, `s` usua
lly a string or source column, `x` and `y` dates.                               - `n`, `start` and `len` are integer literals; `lit` is a literal.
- `i` is a column of positions, `g` a group set, `key` a [sort key](sorting.md#s
ort-keys), `table.column` a stored column.                                      
Where an element-wise instruction takes a register operand, a literal may be use
d instead; it stands for that value at every row ([literals](../language.md#literals)).                                                                         
Positions are 0-based INT values.

An operand that expects a column can't name a group set, and the reverse; either
is an error, as is reading a register that hasn't been set.

## Element-wise instructions

The instructions on the [arithmetic](arithmetic.md), [logic](logic.md), [strings
](strings.md) and [dates](dates.md) pages compute one result value per row:     
- All register operands must have the same length, which is the result's length.
- At least one operand must be a register.
- Unless noted, the result is `NULL` when any operand is `NULL`. That comes firs
t: `DIV` of NULL by 0 is NULL, not division by zero, and `ADD` of NULL and a STR is NULL, not a type error.                                                     - Types are checked row by row: an operand of the wrong type is an error only at
 a row where the instruction uses it, so whether a program fails can depend on its data. An empty column, or one of NULLs, never gives a type error.            
Given a table `t` whose INT column `x` holds `1`, `NULL`, `3`:

```text
LOAD  x, t.x
ADD   y, x, 10      ; the literal 10 stands for 10 at every row
OUT   y
```

prints `{"ncols":1,"rows":[[11],[null],[13]],"cycles":18}`.

## Index

### Arithmetic

| Instruction | Summary |
|---|---|
| [`ADD`](arithmetic.md#add-sub-mul) | sum |
| [`SUB`](arithmetic.md#add-sub-mul) | difference |
| [`MUL`](arithmetic.md#add-sub-mul) | product |
| [`DIV`](arithmetic.md#div) | NUM quotient |
| [`IDIV`](arithmetic.md#idiv) | INT quotient truncated toward zero |
| [`MOD`](arithmetic.md#mod) | INT remainder with the sign of `a` |
| [`NEG`](arithmetic.md#neg) | negation |
| [`WRAP`](arithmetic.md#wrap) | INT wrapped to 32-bit two's complement |
| [`TRUNC`](arithmetic.md#trunc) | NUM truncated toward zero to INT |

### Logic

| Instruction | Summary |
|---|---|
| [`EQ`](logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) | equal |
| [`NE`](logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) | not equal |
| [`LT`](logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) | less than |
| [`LE`](logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) | less than or equal |
| [`GT`](logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) | greater than |
| [`GE`](logic.md#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) | greater than or equal |
| [`IS`](logic.md#is) | equal, or both NULL; never NULL |
| [`AND`](logic.md#and-or) | three-valued conjunction |
| [`OR`](logic.md#and-or) | three-valued disjunction |
| [`NOT`](logic.md#not) | BOOL negation |
| [`ISNULL`](logic.md#isnull) | whether the value is NULL |
| [`NVL`](logic.md#nvl) | `a`, or `b` when `a` is NULL |
| [`IF`](logic.md#if) | `a` where `c` is TRUE, else `b` |
| [`NULLIF`](logic.md#nullif) | NULL where `a IS b`, else `a` |
| [`NULLIFE`](logic.md#nullife) | NULL where `a` is the empty string, else `a` |

### Strings

| Instruction | Summary |
|---|---|
| [`UPPER`](strings.md#upper) | upper case |
| [`RTRIM`](strings.md#rtrim-trim) | without trailing spaces |
| [`TRIM`](strings.md#rtrim-trim) | without leading and trailing spaces |
| [`LEFT`](strings.md#left) | first `n` characters |
| [`SUBSTR`](strings.md#substr) | `len` characters from 1-based `start` |
| [`LEN`](strings.md#len) | number of characters |
| [`CAT`](strings.md#cat) | concatenation |

### Dates

| Instruction | Summary |
|---|---|
| [`YEAR`](dates.md#year-month-day) | year |
| [`MONTH`](dates.md#year-month-day) | month |
| [`DAY`](dates.md#year-month-day) | day of month |
| [`DOW`](dates.md#dow) | day of week, 1 = Monday ... 7 = Sunday |
| [`DATEADD`](dates.md#dateadd) | date plus `n` days |
| [`DATEDIFF`](dates.md#datediff) | days from `y` to `x` |

### Columns

| Instruction | Summary |
|---|---|
| [`LOAD`](columns.md#load) | a stored column |
| [`FILL`](columns.md#fill) | a literal repeated once per value of `s` |
| [`IOTA`](columns.md#iota) | positions `0 .. len(s)-1` |
| [`IDX`](columns.md#idx) | positions where a BOOL column is TRUE |
| [`GATHER`](columns.md#gather) | `d[k] = s[i[k]]` |
| [`SLICE`](columns.md#slice) | the first `n` values |
| [`OUT`](columns.md#out) | the program's result |

### Sorting

| Instruction | Summary |
|---|---|
| [`SORT`](sorting.md#sort) | positions of the rows in stable sorted order |
| [`TOPK`](sorting.md#topk) | the first `n` positions of that order |

Sort keys are described in [Sort keys](sorting.md#sort-keys).

### Joins

|---|---|
| [`NLJOIN`](joins.md#nljoin-hjoin) | positions of all pairs with equal keys |
| [`HJOIN`](joins.md#nljoin-hjoin) | same result as `NLJOIN` |

### Grouping

| Instruction | Summary |
|---|---|
| [`GROUP`](grouping.md#group) | group set of rows with equal keys |
| [`GALL`](grouping.md#gall) | one group holding every row |

| [`GFIRST`](grouping.md#gfirst) | position of each group's first row |
| [`GCOUNT`](grouping.md#gcount) | rows per group |
| [`GCOUNTV`](grouping.md#gcountv) | non-NULL values per group |
| [`GSUM`](grouping.md#gsum) | sum of non-NULL values per group |
| [`GMIN`](grouping.md#gmin-gmax) | least non-NULL value per group |
| [`GMAX`](grouping.md#gmin-gmax) | greatest non-NULL value per group |

# Logic

Element-wise comparisons, BOOL logic and NULL handling. All instructions on this
 page follow the [element-wise rules](README.md#element-wise-instructions); where an instruction's NULL behavior differs from the default (the result is `NULL` when any operand is `NULL`), its section says so.                               
| Instruction | Result |
|---|---|
| [`EQ` `NE` `LT` `LE` `GT` `GE` `d, a, b`](#eq-ne-lt-le-gt-ge) | BOOL compariso
n |                                                                             | [`IS d, a, b`](#is) | BOOL, never NULL: equal, or both NULL |
| [`AND d, a, b`](#and-or) / `OR` | three-valued logic |
| [`NOT d, a`](#not) | BOOL negation |
| [`ISNULL d, a`](#isnull) | BOOL, never NULL |
| [`NVL d, a, b`](#nvl) | `a`, or `b` when `a` is NULL |
| [`IF d, c, a, b`](#if) | `a` where `c` is TRUE, else `b` |
| [`NULLIF d, a, b`](#nullif) | NULL where `a IS b`, else `a` |
| [`NULLIFE d, a`](#nullife) | NULL where `a` is the empty string, else `a` |

## `EQ`, `NE`, `LT`, `LE`, `GT`, `GE`

```text
EQ d, a, b
NE d, a, b
LT d, a, b
LE d, a, b
GT d, a, b
GE d, a, b
```

BOOL comparison of `a` with `b`: `a = b`, `a <> b`, `a < b`, `a <= b`, `a > b`, 
`a >= b`. Values are ordered as described in [Ordering](../values.md#ordering); comparing other mixes of types is an error.                                     
**Cycles:** 1 per element, plus the bytes of the shorter operand ([rules](../cyc
les.md#string-bytes)).                                                          
## `IS`

```text
IS d, a, b
```

BOOL, never NULL: TRUE where `a` and `b` are equal, or both NULL, and FALSE wher
e just one is NULL. Values are ordered as described in [Ordering](../values.md#ordering); comparing two non-NULL values of other mixes of types is an error.    
**Cycles:** 1 per element, plus the bytes of the shorter operand ([rules](../cyc
les.md#string-bytes)).                                                          
## `AND`, `OR`

```text
AND d, a, b
OR  d, a, b
```

Three-valued logic on BOOL values; a non-BOOL operand is an error: `FALSE AND NU
LL` is `FALSE`, and `TRUE OR NULL` is `TRUE`; otherwise a NULL operand gives NULL.                                                                              
| `a` | `b` | `AND` | `OR` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `TRUE` | `TRUE` | `TRUE` | `TRUE` |
| `TRUE` | `FALSE` | `FALSE` | `TRUE` |
| `FALSE` | `FALSE` | `FALSE` | `FALSE` |
| `TRUE` | `NULL` | `NULL` | `TRUE` |
| `FALSE` | `NULL` | `FALSE` | `NULL` |
| `NULL` | `NULL` | `NULL` | `NULL` |

Both instructions are symmetric in `a` and `b`.

**Cycles:** 1 per element.

## `NOT`

```text
NOT d, a
```

BOOL negation of `a`, which must be BOOL.

**Cycles:** 1 per element.

## `ISNULL`

```text
ISNULL d, a
```

BOOL, never NULL: TRUE where `a` is NULL.

**Cycles:** 1 per element; no string bytes.

## `NVL`

```text
NVL d, a, b
```

`a`, or `b` where `a` is NULL. `a` and `b` may have different types.

**Cycles:** 1 per element; no string bytes.

## `IF`

```text
IF d, c, a, b
```

`a` where `c` is TRUE, else `b` (also where `c` is NULL). `c` must be BOOL; `a` 
and `b` may have any types, and a NULL `a` or `b` is passed through.            
**Cycles:** 1 per element; no string bytes.

## `NULLIF`

```text
NULLIF d, a, b
```

NULL where `a IS b` (see [`IS`](#is)), else `a`.

**Cycles:** 1 per element; no string bytes.

## `NULLIFE`

```text
NULLIFE d, a
```

NULL where `a` is the empty string, else `a`, which must be STR.

**Cycles:** 1 per element; no string bytes.
[MiniVM docs](../README.md) › [Instructions](README.md) › Arithmetic

# Arithmetic

Element-wise arithmetic on INT and NUM values. All instructions on this page fol
low the [element-wise rules](README.md#element-wise-instructions): the result is `NULL` when any operand is `NULL`. Their operands and results are numbers, so they pay no [string bytes](../cycles.md#string-bytes).                           
| Instruction | Result |
|---|---|
| [`ADD d, a, b`](#add-sub-mul) / `SUB` / `MUL` | INT if both are INT, else NUM 
|                                                                               | [`DIV d, a, b`](#div) | NUM quotient |
| [`IDIV d, a, b`](#idiv) | INT quotient truncated toward zero |
| [`MOD d, a, b`](#mod) | INT remainder with the sign of `a` |
| [`NEG d, a`](#neg) | `-a` |
| [`WRAP d, a`](#wrap) | INT wrapped to 32-bit two's complement |
| [`TRUNC d, a`](#trunc) | INT |

## `ADD`, `SUB`, `MUL`

```text
ADD d, a, b
SUB d, a, b
MUL d, a, b
```

`a + b`, `a - b` and `a * b`. The result is INT if both operands are INT, else N
UM, rounded as in [NUM range](../values.md#num-range). A result outside the INT or NUM range is the error `numeric overflow`, as is an INT operand above 2^96 - 1 in magnitude when the other operand is NUM.                                   
**Cycles:** 1 per element.

## `DIV`

```text
DIV d, a, b
```

The NUM quotient `a / b`, rounded as in [NUM range](../values.md#num-range), eve
n when both operands are INT. It is an error if `b` is 0, and `numeric overflow` if the quotient is outside the NUM range or an INT operand is above 2^96 - 1 in magnitude.                                                                     
**Cycles:** 6 per element.

## `IDIV`

```text
IDIV d, a, b
```

The INT quotient `a / b`, truncated toward zero. Both operands must be INT. It i
s an error if `b` is 0, or if the quotient is outside the INT range.            
**Cycles:** 6 per element.

## `MOD`

```text
MOD d, a, b
```

The INT remainder of `a / b`, with the sign of `a`. Both operands must be INT. I
t is an error if `b` is 0.                                                      
**Cycles:** 6 per element.

## `NEG`

```text
NEG d, a
```

`-a`. A result outside the INT or NUM range is an error.

**Cycles:** 1 per element.

## `WRAP`

```text
WRAP d, a
```

INT `a` wrapped to 32-bit two's complement.

**Cycles:** 1 per element.

## `TRUNC`

```text
TRUNC d, a
```

INT: a NUM `a` truncated toward zero; an INT `a` is unchanged. Any other type is
 an error.                                                                      
**Cycles:** 2 per element.
[MiniVM docs](../README.md) › [Instructions](README.md) › Strings

# Strings

Element-wise operations on STR values. All instructions on this page follow the 
[element-wise rules](README.md#element-wise-instructions): the result is `NULL` when any operand is `NULL`. Lengths and positions count characters; string-byte costs count bytes ([rules](../cycles.md#string-bytes)).                         
| Instruction | Result |
|---|---|
| [`UPPER d, s`](#upper) | upper case (Unicode) |
| [`RTRIM d, s`](#rtrim-trim) / [`TRIM d, s`](#rtrim-trim) | without trailing / 
leading and trailing spaces |                                                   | [`LEFT d, s, n`](#left) | first `n` characters |
| [`SUBSTR d, s, start, len`](#substr) | `len` characters from 1-based `start` |
| [`LEN d, s`](#len) | number of characters |
| [`CAT d, a, b`](#cat) | concatenation |

## `UPPER`

```text
UPPER d, s
```

`s` in upper case, by Unicode's full case mapping, which can change the number o
f characters: `UPPER('straße')` is `'STRASSE'`.                                 
**Cycles:** 1 per element, plus 1 per byte of `s` and of the result ([rules](../
cycles.md#string-bytes)).                                                       
## `RTRIM`, `TRIM`

```text
RTRIM d, s
TRIM  d, s
```

`s` without trailing spaces (`RTRIM`), or without leading and trailing spaces (`
TRIM`). Only `' '` counts as a space.                                           
**Cycles:** 1 per element, plus 1 per byte of `s` and of the result ([rules](../
cycles.md#string-bytes)).                                                       
## `LEFT`

```text
LEFT d, s, n
```

The first `n` characters of `s` (all of `s` if it is shorter). `n` is a non-nega
tive [integer literal](../language.md#integer-operands).                        
**Cycles:** 1 per element, plus 1 per byte of `s` and of the result ([rules](../
cycles.md#string-bytes)).                                                       
## `SUBSTR`

[MiniVM docs](../README.md) › [Instructions](README.md) › Sorting

# Sorting instructions

`SORT` and `TOPK` order the rows of one or more key columns and return positions
, which [`GATHER`](columns.md#gather) applies to any column of the same rows. Positions are 0-based INT values ([notation](README.md#notation)).                
| Instruction | Result |
|---|---|
| [`SORT d, key, ...`](#sort) | positions of the rows in stable sorted order |
| [`TOPK d, n, key, ...`](#topk) | the first `n` positions of the same order |

## `SORT`

```text
SORT d, key, ...
```

Sets `d` to the positions of the rows in stable sorted order by the [sort keys](
#sort-keys).                                                                    
**Cycles:** 2 per row, plus every comparison of a stable top-down merge sort ([c
omparison cost](../cycles.md#comparisons)).                                     
## `TOPK`

```text
TOPK d, n, key, ...
```

Sets `d` to the first `n` positions of the order `SORT` would produce for the sa
me keys (all of them if there are fewer rows). `n` is an integer literal.       
**Cycles:** 2 per row, plus every comparison of a bounded insertion buffer (each
 row is compared with the current `n`-th, then placed by binary search) ([comparison cost](../cycles.md#comparisons)), plus 1 per buffered row shifted.         
## Sort keys

```text
reg ASC|DESC NF|NL
```

A sort key is a register followed by a direction and a NULL placement, separated
 by spaces or tabs; all three parts are required. All key columns must have the same length. Rows are ordered by the first key, then by each following key among rows the earlier keys leave equal.                                             
- `ASC` orders values from least to greatest, `DESC` reverses the order of value
s. Values are compared as in [Ordering](../values.md#ordering).                 - `NF` puts NULLs first and `NL` puts them last, whatever the direction.
- Ties keep their input order.

Customers by credit, highest first with NULLs last, then by name:

```text
LOAD   name, customers.c_name
LOAD   credit, customers.c_credit
SORT   p, credit DESC NL, name ASC NF
GATHER n, name, p
GATHER c, credit, p
OUT    n, c
```
[MiniVM docs](../README.md) › [Instructions](README.md) › Joins

# Join instructions

`NLJOIN` and `HJOIN` pair up the rows of two key columns whose keys are equal an
d return the pairs as two position columns. Positions are 0-based INT values ([notation](README.md#notation)).                                                  
| Instruction | Result |
|---|---|
| [`NLJOIN li, ri, lk, rk [, NULLEQ]`](#nljoin-hjoin) | positions of all pairs w
ith `lk[i] = rk[j]` |                                                           | [`HJOIN li, ri, lk, rk [, NULLEQ]`](#nljoin-hjoin) | same result as `NLJOIN` |

## `NLJOIN`, `HJOIN`

```text
NLJOIN li, ri, lk, rk [, NULLEQ]
HJOIN  li, ri, lk, rk [, NULLEQ]
```

Finds all pairs `(i, j)` with `lk[i] = rk[j]`, ordered by `i` then `j`. Sets `li
` to the positions into `lk` and `ri` to the positions into `rk`, one entry per pair; if `li` and `ri` are the same register, it holds the positions into `rk`. Keys are compared as in [Ordering](../values.md#ordering): a non-NULL left key that can't be compared with a non-NULL right key (e.g. STR with INT) is an error. A NULL key matches no key, unless the optional `NULLEQ` flag is given, in which case NULL keys match each other. `HJOIN` gives the same result as `NLJOIN`, errors included; only the cost differs.                                            
**Cycles (`NLJOIN`):** per pair of rows: 1 plus the bytes of the shorter string 
key ([rules](../cycles.md#string-bytes)); plus 2 per output pair.               
**Cycles (`HJOIN`):** per row of either side: 6 plus its key's string bytes ([ru
les](../cycles.md#string-bytes)); plus 2 per output pair.                       
### Example

[`GATHER`](columns.md#gather) through `li` picks columns of the left rows and th
rough `ri` columns of the right rows, giving one row per pair. Customers with their region's name:                                                              
```text
LOAD   reg, customers.c_region
LOAD   code, regions.r_code
HJOIN  li, ri, reg, code
LOAD   cname, customers.c_name
LOAD   rname, regions.r_name
GATHER c, cname, li
GATHER r, rname, ri
OUT    c, r
```

On `examples/data.json` this prints `[["Cy","Southern"],["Dee","West Coast"],["E
ve","Southern"], ...]`.                                                         [MiniVM docs](../README.md) › [Instructions](README.md) › Grouping

# Grouping instructions

`GROUP` and `GALL` divide rows into groups and store them as a group set; the ot
her instructions on this page read a group set and return columns. Positions are 0-based INT values ([notation](README.md#notation)).                           
| Instruction | Result |
|---|---|
| [`GROUP g, k, ...`](#group) | group set: rows with equal keys share a group |
| [`GALL g, s`](#gall) | group set: one group holding every row of `s` |
| [`GID d, g`](#gid) | group number of each row |
| [`GFIRST d, g`](#gfirst) | position of each group's first row |
| [`GCOUNT d, g`](#gcount) | rows per group |
| [`GCOUNTV d, g, s`](#gcountv) | non-NULL values of `s` per group |
| [`GSUM d, g, s`](#gsum) | sum of non-NULL values per group |
| [`GMIN d, g, s` / `GMAX`](#gmin-gmax) | least / greatest non-NULL value per gr
oup |                                                                           
## Group sets

A register holds either a column or a group set ([values](../values.md#columns-a
nd-group-sets)). A group set assigns each of its rows a group number; groups are numbered from 0 in order of first appearance. [`GROUP`](#group) and [`GALL`](#gall) produce a group set. [`GID`](#gid) returns a column with one value per row; the aggregates [`GFIRST`](#gfirst) through [`GMAX`](#gmin-gmax) return a column with one value per group, the value for group `k` at position `k`. The `s` operand of an aggregate is a column over the same rows as the group set; a different length is an error.                                                            
Aggregate columns of the same group set line up with each other. To label each g
roup with its key, gather the key at [`GFIRST`](#gfirst). Orders per status:    
```text
LOAD   st, orders.o_status
GROUP  g, st
GFIRST f, g
GATHER key, st, f
GCOUNT n, g
OUT    key, n
```

On `examples/data.json` this prints `[["open",7],["closed",12],["shipped",11]]`.

## `GROUP`

```text
GROUP g, k, ...
```

Sets `g` to a group set over the rows of the key columns `k, ...`: rows with equ
al keys share a group, and NULL equals NULL. All key columns must have the same length. Keys are compared as in [Ordering](../values.md#ordering): INT and NUM mix (`1` and `1.00` share a group), and a key column holding values that can't be compared (e.g. STR and INT) is an error.                                       
**Cycles:** per row: 6 plus the string bytes of its keys ([rules](../cycles.md#s
tring-bytes)).                                                                  
## `GALL`

```text
GALL g, s
```

Sets `g` to a group set with one group holding every row of `s`, even when `s` i
s empty.                                                                        
**Cycles:** 1 per row.

## `GID`

```text
GID d, g
```

Sets `d` to the group number of each row of `g`.

**Cycles:** 1 per row.

## `GFIRST`

```text
GFIRST d, g
```

Sets `d` to the position of each group's first row. The result is NULL for the g
roup of an empty `GALL`.                                                        
**Cycles:** 1 per row.

## `GCOUNT`

```text
GCOUNT d, g
```

Sets `d` to the number of rows in each group.

**Cycles:** 2 per row.

## `GCOUNTV`

```text
GCOUNTV d, g, s
```

Sets `d` to the number of non-NULL values of `s` in each group.

**Cycles:** 2 per row.

## `GSUM`

```text
GSUM d, g, s
```

Sets `d` to the sum of the non-NULL values of `s` in each group: INT when all ar
e INT, else NUM. The result is NULL for a group with no non-NULL values. A NUM sum is computed exactly, with as many digits after the point as the value with the most, and rounded once as in [NUM range](../values.md#num-range), so it doesn't depend on the order of the rows. Only each group's total is checked: a total outside the INT or NUM range is the error `numeric overflow`, whatever the running sums along the way.                                                           
**Cycles:** 2 per row.

## `GMIN`, `GMAX`

```text
GMIN d, g, s
GMAX d, g, s
```

Sets `d` to the least (`GMIN`) or greatest (`GMAX`) non-NULL value of `s` in eac
h group, the first of equals: of `1`, `1.0` and `1.00`, whichever comes first. Values are compared as in [Ordering](../values.md#ordering). The result is NULL for a group with no non-NULL values.                                             
**Cycles:** 2 per row, plus the bytes of each non-NULL string ([rules](../cycles
.md#string-bytes)).                                                             [MiniVM docs](../README.md) › [Instructions](README.md) › Columns

# Column instructions

These instructions load table columns, build columns, select and reorder values 
by position, and produce the program's result. They are not element-wise. Positions are 0-based INT values ([notation](README.md#notation)).                    
| Instruction | Result |
|---|---|
| [`LOAD d, table.column`](#load) | the column as stored |
| [`FILL d, lit, s`](#fill) | `lit` repeated once per value of `s` |
| [`IOTA d, s`](#iota) | positions `0 .. len(s)-1` |
| [`IDX d, s`](#idx) | positions where `s` is TRUE |
| [`GATHER d, s, i`](#gather) | `d[k] = s[i[k]]` |
| [`SLICE d, s, n`](#slice) | the first `n` values of `s` |
| [`OUT s, ...`](#out) | the program's result |

## `LOAD`

```text
LOAD d, table.column
```

Sets `d` to the column `column` of table `table` as stored. An empty string stay
s `''`; it is not NULL.                                                         
**Cycles:** 1 per value produced.

## `FILL`

```text
FILL d, lit, s
```

Sets `d` to the literal `lit` repeated once per value of `s`. `lit` must be a li
teral.                                                                          
**Cycles:** 1 per value produced.

## `IOTA`

```text
IOTA d, s
```

Sets `d` to the positions `0 .. len(s)-1` of `s`.

**Cycles:** 1 per value produced.

## `IDX`

```text
IDX d, s
```

Sets `d` to the positions, in order, where the BOOL column `s` is TRUE. FALSE an
d NULL positions are left out.                                                  
**Cycles:** 1 per input value.

## `GATHER`

```text
GATHER d, s, i
```

Sets `d[k] = s[i[k]]` for every position `k` of `i`; `d` has the length of `i`. 
Every index must be an INT in range for `s`, or the instruction is an error. Use it with the positions from [`IDX`](#idx), [`SORT`](sorting.md#sort), [`TOPK`](sorting.md#topk), the [joins](joins.md#nljoin-hjoin) and [`GFIRST`](grouping.md#gfirst) to filter, reorder, pair up or pick rows.                                
**Cycles:** 1 per value produced.

## `SLICE`

```text
SLICE d, s, n
```

Sets `d` to the first `n` values of `s` (all of `s` if it has fewer). `n` is an 
integer literal.                                                                
**Cycles:** 1 per value produced.

## `OUT`

```text
OUT s, ...
```

Produces the program's result: one column per operand, all the same length. `OUT
` must be the last instruction and the program's only `OUT` ([program rules](../running.md#program-rules)).                                                     
**Cycles:** nothing beyond the base cost.

I'm noting the CPU usage suggests something's bound by core count, and the quick schema only has a handful of example datasets, which is fine. My plan is to write a fakes module with many transform modes over parsed programs, then build a meta-evaluation script that runs the quick evaluation against each fake, weighing whether to run them in parallel or sequentially given the per-run cost and total count.

Now I'm carefully designing each fake's honesty level: identity, dead-code elimination, renaming, formatting, join-swap, tiny-drift, scaling, and hand-optimized variants are all clearly honest transforms. I'm also considering a case-randomization fake for opcodes and keywords, and a trickier one that appends an extra sort key to reverse tie-breaking order after a stable sort — questioning whether this counts as honest given the spec's ambiguity about whether tie order counts as "specified" by the program.

But I realize this tie-reorder fake is risky: if the sorted output later feeds into a GROUP with GFIRST, reordering ties changes which row gets picked first in each group, which then changes what GATHER retrieves — that's a genuine semantic defect, not a harmless reordering. So I need to restrict this fake to only apply when the sort's output positions are directly consumed by operations that don't care about tie order, to keep it truly honest.

I'm realizing a filter instruction placed after SLICE could break the WARN path's length-matching requirement, since tie-breaking differences would produce mismatched row counts rather than equivalent reordered blocks. So I should tighten the rule to exclude IDX filters appearing after a SLICE, limiting the allowed post-sort instructions to just GATHER and SLICE themselves.

I also need to add a tiebreak key to TOPK similarly, and think through other honest-fake heuristics: swapping hash join for nested-loop join, hoisting independent LOADs to the top after SSA renaming for safety, and deduplicating identical LOAD instructions as a basic CSE pass.

For sort elimination, I want to detect when a SORT is applied to a table already sorted by that exact key prefix with ASC NF semantics — in that case the sort is just an identity permutation equal to IOTA, so I can replace it safely, as long as the sort keys come from raw LOADs rather than gathered values.

Beyond that, I'm cataloging more candidate rewrites: normalizing keyword case for asc/nf/null, letting int-as-num handle tiny drift/scale cases, expanding double negation trivially, and considering dropping NVL on columns that are already guaranteed not-null since the datagen never produces nulls there (making that removal safe). I'm also starting to think about converting GE comparisons on integers into GT equivalents where it's provably equivalent.

Then I shift to designing the buggy counterparts: making NVL drop effectively a no-op that misfires when the value is actually null, flipping all GE comparisons to GT universally (not just the first instance), and turning a not-null filter check into something that always evaluates true instead of actually checking.

I also consider swapping join sides—reversing the order of left/right keys—which produces the same result set but potentially changes row order, meaning it's only truly buggy if there's an earlier sort whose ordering matters before the join executes.

Actually GFIRST after swap could break things since which row counts as "first" changes, risking different gathered values downstream — too risky to keep this as a safe honest transform, so I'll drop h_join_commute entirely and move to a simpler candidate: decrementing TOPK's n by one when n is positive.

I also want a mutation that strips a DIV-guarding filter — tracing an IDX whose output transitively feeds a DIV's divisor, then removing that guard so it introduces a division error.

For deduplicating a no-key table, the fake could swap row selection with a distinct-rows pass after loading, though that gets complex to implement cleanly.

I need to check which table lacks a key — maybe m06_customers_nokey — and make sure datagen actually produces duplicate rows for no-key tables rather than just duplicate column values, since that's what would expose the assume-distinct bug.

For the filter-above-slice bug, I'm now thinking through how to generically detect and transform a SLICE followed by a later IDX filter so the filter gets pushed before the slice — this is tricky to implement generically, so I'm considering just removing the SLICE instruction entirely as a simpler mutation.

I realize progen's standard idiom finishes with sort+slice last, so the real bug case arises when the original program instead does top-N then filters afterward. I'll add that as a specific progen idiom to target for the buggy fake.

So the fake becomes: drop the early slice, run the filter over the full gathered set, then apply the slice-by-n at the very end to each output column. This diverges from the original whenever the filter removes rows among the first n, since taking the first n before filtering yields a different result than filtering first and taking the first n after.

For the GSUM/GCOUNT bug, I'm thinking of swapping a grouped-sum aggregation for a grouped-count instead, which should produce a clearly wrong but structurally similar result.

For string literal case mutations, I'm planning to flip the case of letter literals in comparisons—uppercasing lowercase ones, lowercasing already-uppercase ones via toggle logic, while leaving non-letter strings like 'NULL' untouched.

I'm also considering an "emit invalid program" fault that deliberately breaks output, maybe by dropping the OUT statement or injecting garbage, applied probabilistically to a subset of programs rather than all of them.

For the sleep-delay fault, I want it triggered for roughly one in ten programs deterministically (hashing the basename), while also guaranteeing it fires for at least one known test case like q0003, so the fault is reliably exercised without slowing down the whole suite.

Beyond that I'm considering more buggy variants: silently dropping NULLEQ joins, converting IS comparisons to plain EQ (which breaks NULL handling since IS NULL would wrongly become NULL-propagating EQ), and swapping GALL for GROUP so single-row aggregate results get split by distinct value instead of collapsed.

I also find a sharper empty-table catch: replacing GALL with GROUP over a filled constant column, which matches everywhere except when the input is empty, where GALL yields one row but GROUP yields zero. Another idea is replacing boolean AND with an IF expression that mimics three-valued logic in most cases but diverges when NULL is combined with FALSE or TRUE.

Checking other candidates — NE vs NOT(EQ) is semantically identical so I'd skip that, and UPPER or LEFT/SUBSTR variants don't offer any real behavioral difference to exploit either.

More promising mutations: swapping NF/NL in the first sort key (only detectable when nulls appear in sort data), shifting a date literal by one day in comparisons to test boundary conditions, bumping an integer literal by one in comparisons, dropping RTRIM as a no-op, or silently adding DISTINCT behavior to remove duplicate rows via grouping.

I'm also considering truncating large outputs to catch bugs only visible with big datasets, reordering CAT arguments, and exploiting stats-based assumptions by replacing filters with literals derived from known min/max bounds.

For the always-false case I'd want something like replacing the comparison with an ISNULL check ANDed with FALSE, since the literals in generated programs often come straight from stats bounds, making this bug trigger reliably.

Beyond that, I'm cataloging more honest-optimization candidates: the integer GE/GT rewrite, sorting-on-already-sorted detection, load hoisting during scheduling, and common subexpression elimination.

The TOPK rewrite works if I replace SORT+keys with a bounded TOPK when a later SLICE with matching length n exists and nothing between them filters the rows, keeping the subsequent IOTA/SLICE/GATHER valid. For h_dead_div, I'm considering inserting a harmless DIV by the literal 1 after loading a numeric column, since dividing by one is always safe and leaves the result unused.

I'm also sketching another honest fake, h_reverse_unordered, which reverses output rows only when the program lacks any SORT or TOPK — since no explicit ordering means row order is unspecified and reversing it stays faithful to multiset semantics. Now I'm shifting to planning the meta-evaluation step, writing wrapper scripts in a temp directory to run the fakes and surface where the evaluator's weaknesses actually lie.

I'm weighing timing concerns: python startup overhead is small relative to the optimizer's 1-second limit, but running multiple meta-evals in parallel risks false timeout alarms under CPU contention, so I'll cap parallelism at around three concurrent runs to stay safe, while things like b_sleep's 1.5s delay should still get caught reliably.

I also need the fakes to handle schema-dependent cases like dedup without keys, sorting on sorted input, and stats, with the schema passed in as the second argument. Let me check an example schema plus some sample programs and test cases to get a feel for the conventions used.

For the tie-reorder transform, I need to locate the last SORT/TOPK instruction and verify the tail only contains safe ops like GATHER, SLICE, IOTA, IDX, elementwise, OUT, FILL, LOAD, skipping if grouping or joins appear afterward—then I can safely append a reversed tiebreaker key backed by an injected IOTA register to flip tie ordering without producing anything beyond a benign WARN.

For sort-on-already-sorted detection, I'm tracking which registers were loaded directly from a column (invalidated on redefinition), then checking if a SORT's key columns form a prefix of the table's known sort order with ascending-no-flags semantics—if so, the sort is a no-op and can be replaced by an identity IOTA, since stable sorting on a prefix preserves the existing tie-breaking from the remaining sorted suffix.

I'm also drafting range-comparison simplifications: GE against an integer-loaded register becomes GT with the literal decremented by one, and LE similarly becomes LT with the literal incremented by one, both honest rewrites for integer-typed loads. For dropping redundant NVL calls on known not-null columns, I'm trying to find a clean no-op replacement, considering options like gathering a copy or simplifying NVL's fallback to NULL since the input is guaranteed non-null anyway.

For hoisting loads, I need to convert the program to SSA form first — giving each definition a unique versioned name, tracking current bindings for uses, and collapsing joins where branches agree on the same value. Once in SSA, I can safely move all LOAD instructions to the top since they have no dependencies, and then for common subexpression elimination I can alias duplicate LOADs of the same table/column to the first occurrence and drop the redundant instruction, substituting uses accordingly.

For the top-k-from-slice pattern, I'm working out detection logic: find a SORT producing permutation p, then later a SLICE whose source traces back through GATHER/IOTA operations derived from p, with no intervening IDX/GROUP/GALL/JOIN/SORT/TOPK instructions in between — essentially tracking the domain of registers reachable from p to confirm the slice is operating on the sorted order.

But I realize there's a correctness risk: if any register in that domain is used later without being sliced (e.g. passed directly to OUT or GROUP), replacing SORT with TOPK would break semantics since TOPK only preserves the top n rows. I'm trying to restrict the rule so that after the SLICE, domain registers can only be used as gather sources with the sliced index — otherwise the optimization isn't safe.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Meta-evaluation: test ./evaluate against every fake optimizer in tools/fakes.py.

  meta_eval.py [MODE ...] [--seed S] [--full] [-j N] [--seeds 1,2,3] [--out runs/meta_report.md]

  buggy fake + evaluate exit != 0 -> CAUGHT      buggy fake + exit 0 -> MISSED
  honest fake + evaluate exit 0   -> OK          honest fake + exit != 0 -> FALSE ALARM

--seeds runs every fake under each seed (a buggy fake counts as CAUGHT only if caught
under every seed; an honest fake is a FALSE ALARM if flagged under any seed).
Writes a markdown report (default runs/meta_report.md). Exit 0 iff 0 missed and 0 false alarms.
"""
import argparse
import json
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
REPO = os.path.dirname(HERE)
sys.path.insert(0, HERE)
import fakes  # noqa: E402


def wrapper(tmp, mode):
    p = os.path.join(tmp, mode + ".sh")
    with open(p, "w") as f:
        f.write(f'#!/bin/sh\nexec "{sys.executable}" "{os.path.join(HERE, "fakes.py")}" {mode} "$@"\n')
    os.chmod(p, 0o755)
    return p


def run_one(tmp, mode, seed, full):
    js = os.path.join(tmp, f"{mode}_{seed}.json")
    cmd = [os.path.join(REPO, "evaluate"), wrapper(tmp, mode), "--seed", str(seed),
           "--json", js, "--keep", os.path.join(tmp, f"keep_{mode}_{seed}")]
    if not full:
        cmd.append("--quick")
    t = time.monotonic()
    r = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, cwd=tmp)
    rep = json.load(open(js)) if os.path.exists(js) else {}
    lines = r.stdout.strip().splitlines()
    return {"rc": r.returncode, "summary": lines[-1] if lines else r.stderr.strip()[-300:],
            "first": [x for x in lines if x.startswith("DEFECT")][:3], "defects": rep.get("defects"),
            "checked": rep.get("checked"), "wall": round(time.monotonic() - t, 1)}


def main(argv):
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("modes", nargs="*")
    ap.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=1)
    ap.add_argument("--seeds")
    ap.add_argument("--full", action="store_true")
    ap.add_argument("-j", type=int, default=3)
    ap.add_argument("--out", default=os.path.join(REPO, "runs", "meta_report.md"))
    a = ap.parse_args(argv)
    modes = a.modes or list(fakes.MODES)
    seeds = [int(x) for x in a.seeds.split(",")] if a.seeds else [a.seed]
    t0 = time.monotonic()
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix="minivm_meta_") as tmp:
        jobs = [(m, s) for m in modes for s in seeds]
        with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=a.j) as ex:
            res = dict(zip(jobs, ex.map(lambda j: run_one(tmp, j[0], j[1], a.full), jobs)))
    tally = {"CAUGHT": 0, "MISSED": 0, "OK": 0, "FALSE ALARM": 0}
    rows = []
    for m in modes:
        kind, desc, _ = fakes.MODES[m]
        rs = [res[(m, s)] for s in seeds]
        flagged = [r["rc"] != 0 for r in rs]
        if kind == "buggy":
            v = "CAUGHT" if all(flagged) else "MISSED"
        else:
            v = "FALSE ALARM" if any(flagged) else "OK"
        tally[v] += 1
        rows.append((m, kind, v, "/".join(str(r["defects"]) for r in rs), desc, rs))
        print(f"{v:<12} {m:<16} {kind:<6} defects={rows[-1][3]:<10} {desc}", flush=True)
        if v in ("MISSED", "FALSE ALARM"):
            for r in rs:
                print("             " + r["summary"])
                for x in r["first"]:
                    print("             " + x)
    wall = time.monotonic() - t0
    nb = sum(1 for r in rows if r[1] == "buggy")
    nh = len(rows) - nb
    total = (f"buggy: caught {tally['CAUGHT']}/{nb}, missed {tally['MISSED']} | honest: ok {tally['OK']}/{nh}, "
             f"false alarms {tally['FALSE ALARM']} | seeds {','.join(map(str, seeds))} | "
             f"{'full' if a.full else 'quick'} | meta wall {wall:.0f}s")
    print("\n" + total)
    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(a.out), exist_ok=True)
    with open(a.out, "w") as f:
        f.write("# ./evaluate vs fake optimizers (tools/meta_eval.py)\n\n")
        f.write(total + "\n\n")
        f.write("| Fake | Expected | Result | Defects (per seed) | Checks | Eval wall s | What it does |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n")
        for m, kind, v, d, desc, rs in rows:
            f.write(f"| `{m}` | {'flag' if kind == 'buggy' else 'pass'} | {v} | {d} | "
                    f"{'/'.join(str(r['checked']) for r in rs)} | {'/'.join(str(r['wall']) for r in rs)} | {desc} |\n")
        bad = [r for r in rows if r[2] in ("MISSED", "FALSE ALARM")]
        if bad:
            f.write("\n## Evidence\n\n")
            for m, kind, v, d, desc, rs in bad:
                f.write(f"- `{m}` {v}: " + " / ".join(r["summary"] for r in rs) + "\n")
                for r in rs:
                    for x in r["first"]:
                        f.write(f"  - `{x}`\n")
    return 0 if tally["MISSED"] == tally["FALSE ALARM"] == 0 else 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main(sys.argv[1:]))
